'''Yasunori Nomura''' (born 21 January 1974 - ) is a [[theoretical physicist]] working on particle physics, quantum gravity, and cosmology. He is a professor of physics at [[University of California, Berkeley]], a senior faculty scientist at [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]], a senior research scientist at [[Riken]], and an affiliate member at [[Institute for the Physics and Mathematics of the Universe|Kavli Institute for the Physics and Mathematics of the Universe]]. Since 2015, he has been the director of the [[Berkeley Center for Theoretical Physics]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://bctp.berkeley.edu/index.html|title = Berkeley Center for Theoretical Physics}}</ref>

==Career==
Nomura received his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] from [[University of Tokyo]] (supervisor [[Tsutomu Yanagida]]) in 2000 and became a [[Miller Research Fellows|Miller Research Fellow]] at University of California, Berkeley. In 2002-03 he was an associate scientist at [[Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory]]. In July 2003 he joined the Department of Physics at University of California, Berkeley. In 2017, Nomura was elected a Fellow of the American Physical Society "for pioneering contributions to a variety of areas of particle theory, including gauge unification in extra dimensions, electroweak symmetry breaking, supersymmetric models, dark matter, the multiverse, foundations of quantum mechanics, and black holes."<ref>[https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=2017&unit_id=&institution= APS Fellows 2017]{{in lang|en}}</ref><ref>[https://www.ipmu.jp/en/20171218-APSfellow_Nomura Yasunori Nomura named new American Physical Society Fellow]</ref>

==Work==
Nomura works on particle physics, quantum gravity, and cosmology. He developed [[Grand Unified Theory|theories of grand unification]] in higher dimensional spacetime<ref>
{{Cite journal
| doi = 10.1016/S0003-4916(03)00077-0
| title = Grand unification in higher dimensions
| journal = Annals of Physics
| volume = 306
| pages = 132–156
| year = 2003
| last1 = Hall | first1 = L.J.
| last2 = Nomura | first2 = Y.
| issue = 1
| arxiv=hep-ph/0212134
| bibcode = 2003AnPhy.306..132H| s2cid = 18898831
}}
</ref> and constructed the so-called holographic Higgs model, the first realistic model in which a composite [[Higgs particle]] arises as a [[Pseudo-Goldstone boson|pseudo-Nambu–Goldstone boson]].<ref>
{{Cite journal
| doi = 10.1016/j.nuclphysb.2003.08.027
| title = Higgs as a holographic pseudo-Goldstone boson
| journal = Nuclear Physics
| volume = B671
| pages = 148–174
| year = 2003
| last1 = Contino | first1 = R.
| last2 = Nomura | first2 = Y.
| last3 = Pomarol | first3 = A.
| arxiv=hep-ph/0306259
| bibcode = 2003NuPhB.671..148C| s2cid = 11533871
}}
</ref> He also proposed that the eternally inflating [[multiverse]] is the same thing as [[Many-worlds interpretation|quantum many worlds]].<ref>
{{Cite journal
| doi = 10.1007/JHEP11(2011)063
| title = Physical theories, eternal inflation, and the quantum universe
| journal = Journal of High Energy Physics
| volume = 2011
| pages = 063
| year = 2011
| last1 = Nomura | first1 = Y.
| issue = 11
| arxiv=1104.2324
| bibcode = 2011JHEP...11..063N
| s2cid = 119283262
}}
</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://blogs.discovermagazine.com/cosmicvariance/2011/05/26/are-many-worlds-and-the-multiverse-the-same-idea/#.VWtNSB29Dak|title=Are Many Worlds and the Multiverse the Same Idea?|access-date=2015-06-04|archive-date=2015-04-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150420234318/http://blogs.discovermagazine.com/cosmicvariance/2011/05/26/are-many-worlds-and-the-multiverse-the-same-idea/#.VWtNSB29Dak|url-status=dead}}</ref>
